investigacion.base:
**Bottom line:** Based on what I found, nothing clearly counts yet. No brand-new Travel Health Notice (THN) for a North American country has been confirmed for October 2026. The one possible trigger is the Global Dengue notice, which CDC updated on October 2, 2026 and which lists Costa Rica, Cuba and Panama. Whether an update counts as "newly issued" is the main ambiguity.

**What the CDC notices page says now (last reviewed October 2, 2026)**
- **Level 4:** CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu (North-Kivu) provinces in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) due to the current Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak.
- **Level 3:** Haut-Uélé and Tshopo provinces in the DRC, for the same outbreak.
- **Level 1:** The Global Dengue notice lists Kenya, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Costa Rica, Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Cuba, Ecuador, including the Galápagos Islands, Panama. It is marked Updated Global Dengue October 02, 2026. Costa Rica, Cuba and Panama count as North America under the usual definition, which includes Central America and the Caribbean.
- **Earlier notices still listed (from an older copy of the page):** Chikungunya in Cuba September 26, 2025 and Yellow Fever in Venezuela (March 16, 2026; Venezuela is South America). Neither is new in October.

**Resolution issues**
- The Dengue notice was updated in October, not first issued then. A strict reading of "newly issued" would leave the question unresolved for now. A loose reading, where an update with a new date or added countries counts, could already mean Yes. It's not clear whether Costa Rica, Cuba or Panama were added on October 2 or were already on the list.
- The Ebola notice was updated October 8 (the CDC page refers to the DRC, Uganda and South Sudan). That has nothing to do with North America.

**Base rates and context**
- CDC posts a few new or updated THNs most months. The Americas show up often, because of dengue, chikungunya, Oropouche, yellow fever and measles, and because hurricanes can trigger notices too. The Global Dengue and Global Measles notices are updated roughly every month and often list Caribbean or Central American countries. Countries covered by the global notices often change from one update to the next.
- October is the peak of hurricane season. A major storm hitting a Caribbean country could lead to a disaster notice.
- The new country-specific notices on the page this year have been Old World or South American (DRC meningococcal disease, Mayotte chikungunya, Venezuela yellow fever, Ghana/Liberia mpox).

**Scheduled events before October 31**
- Nothing is formally scheduled. A routine update to the Global Measles or Global Dengue notice is likely before the end of the month. Hurricane season and arbovirus season continue.

**Prediction markets:** I didn't find any.

**Status:** Unresolved on a strict reading. It could already be Yes on a loose reading because of the October 2 Dengue update, and it's quite plausible something else qualifies before October 31.

**Sources:**
- [1](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/notices)
- [2](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/notices.htm)

criterios: This question resolves as **Yes** if a country in North America has a Travel Health Notice (THN) by the Centers for Disease Control at its [THN](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/notices) page newly issued in October 2026.
letra_pequena: No other resolution source will be used in resolving this question.
razonamientos:
- **Time left:** About 20 days remain in October.
- **Status quo:** No on a strict reading. The October 2 Global Dengue notice was *updated*, not newly issued.
- **Reference class:** CDC issues a few new or updated Travel Health Notices in a typical month, but fewer are new notices covering North American countries. I would put the rough full-month base rate for this event around 20–30%.
- **No scenario:** The CDC makes only updates to existing notices, or issues new notices solely for countries outside North America.
- **Yes scenario:** A new outbreak or other health event prompts a new notice naming a Central American or Caribbean country before November.
- **Resolution technicality:** The CDC THN page is the sole source. Whether its October 2 **update** to Global Dengue counts as “newly issued” could decide the question even without another notice.

Probability: 30%

(a) About 20 days remain, from October 11 to October 31, 2026. Resolution depends on what the CDC THN page shows by then.

(b) If nothing changed, the answer would be No on a strict reading. No country-specific notice for a North American country has been newly issued in October. The only October item touching the region is the Global Dengue notice, which was *updated* on October 2 and lists Costa Rica, Cuba and Panama.

(c) Reference class: brand-new country-specific THNs for North American countries, including Central America and the Caribbean. Recent examples are chikungunya in Cuba (September 2025), Oropouche in Cuba (2024) and chikungunya in Nicaragua (August 2026). These come roughly every 1–3 months. That implies about a 20–35% chance that one appears in a given 20-day window. Hurricane season and arbovirus activity push this up slightly.

(d) No scenario: CDC posts only routine updates to the global dengue and measles notices and notices for non-American countries such as the DRC, Uganda and South Sudan. The resolver treats "updated" global notices as not newly issued.

(e) Yes scenario: either of these would do it.
- CDC issues a new country-specific notice, for example chikungunya or Oropouche in a Caribbean or Central American country, or a hurricane-related notice.
- The resolver counts the October 2 Global Dengue update listing Costa Rica, Cuba and Panama.

(f) The key technicality is the phrase "newly issued." The question's background frames the precedent as a distinct new notice (Nicaragua chikungunya), which suggests a global-notice update would not count. A lenient resolver might still count the October-dated dengue entry. The criteria also say "a country in North America has a THN," which leaves some room for a multi-country notice to count. I put moderate probability on the lenient interpretation.

Combining roughly a 25–30% chance of a genuinely new notice with some chance that the dengue update is counted gives a probability somewhat below even.

Probability: 40%

(a) **Time left until outcome is known:** 20 days (from today, October 11, 2026, until October 31, 2026).
(b) **Status quo outcome:** Under the most faithful interpretation of the author's background note (which distinguishes brand-new country notices from routine global updates), the status quo is currently **No**. Under a looser reading that treats the October 2 Global Dengue update as newly issued, it would be Yes.
(c) **Reference class and base rate:** CDC newly issued Travel Health Notices specifically targeting North American countries (Central America, Caribbean, Canada, Mexico). Historically, CDC issues brand-new country-specific notices for North American destinations at an average rate of roughly 2–4 per year. Over a 20-day window, the Poisson arrival rate implies an approximate 12–18% chance of a new notice being posted.
(d) **Scenario resulting in No:** CDC issues no brand-new Travel Health Notices for any North American nation during the remainder of October, and the resolution source strictly evaluates "newly issued" as requiring a distinct new notice rather than routine updates to ongoing global notices (e.g., Global Dengue or Global Measles).
(e) **Scenario resulting in Yes:** Either an unexpected outbreak/natural disaster prompts a newly designated THN for a North American country between October 12 and 31, or the resolving admin deems the October 2, 2026 update to the Global Dengue notice (which includes Costa Rica, Cuba, and Panama) as satisfying "newly issued."
(f) **Technicalities:** The core technicality is the phrase "newly issued." On the CDC THN dashboard, notices carry explicit badges such as "NEW" vs. "UPDATED." The question background specifically cited the August 3, 2026 Nicaragua Chikungunya notice as the benchmark for a new notice, bypassing the Global Dengue notices active at that time, suggesting that global updates are not viewed as newly issued country notices.

Probability: 32%
